doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Pop marketing, MTV and a jazz TV show
summary: His view of sameness in pop and his idea for a cable jazz show.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What’s your feeling about the marketing today of pop music and MTV? Does it strike you one way or the other, about what kids are exposed to?

Yeah I mean I still think that honestly, there’s room for a variety show of some sort. I don’t think it all has to be about 18 to 35. Because 18 or 49 can do the same thing, can coexist. And I think when you look at the early “Saturday Night Lives” they had Miles Davis and they had Preservation Hall Jazz Band and they had Wynton Marsalis, and they were eclectic. They brought just as much rock & roll as they did jazz or folk or whatever. And I think that’s the part of what that statement is about too, and I think I get a little tired, I mean I’m getting older now, and I’m starting to realize that when I go into HMV it’s the same music. That everybody sounds the same. It’s the same angst-ridden girl singer. And it’s the same four guys singing about you girl. All right already. I understand. How about just once we put on Count Basie and played him just as loud? That’s my dream actually is when the other car pulls up with the loud music that I just hit “April in Paris” on my CD player, or “Whirly Bird.” Say oh yeah? Dig this. I’ll blow your speakers right out. It’s just as heavy. And it’s just as rock & roll. And so Preacher John. But I mean I think it takes — somebody is going to figure it out. Maybe never, but I mean I still believe that somebody along the line will go why don’t we have a half hour show at 9:00 on a cable station that says here’s Clark Terry? And then here’s Wallace Roney or here’s John Pizzarelli or here’s Diana Krall. And in a way it just says well they’re going to play music for seven minutes, not three. Not at the end of a show and then get them off. I mean I think people would like that. There’s a way to do it, it’s just we haven’t figured out how to do it and how to like do it so that you can do it economically. That’s the other thing about how are we going to do it. You know you’ve got two cameras. If you had two cameras and a little sound board and you had Diana Krall and you figured it out, you could do it. I don’t think it’s that hard.
